text: That is a fair question. Let me think for a second.
I do not have that number, off the top of my head.
I will get back to you, by tomorrow morning.
If the rate goes up, our cost goes up with it.

I coach executives before board meetings, and the first thing I teach is this: nobody expects you to answer in zero seconds. When a hard question arrives, the mind goes blank for a moment. That is normal. The problem is what people do next. They panic and start talking before they know what they want to say. So I give my clients three or four phrases to buy time. That is a good question. Let me think about that for a second. If I understand you correctly, you are asking about the cost. Three seconds, and the brain comes back. Then you give one point and one reason. Short. And you stop.

I sit on two boards, and I hear those buying-time phrases every week. That is a great question, let me think about it. Honestly, when I hear that three times in one meeting, I stop trusting the answers. It sounds like a technique. What I respect is a person who says, I do not know that number off the top of my head, I will get back to you by tomorrow morning. And then they do. That is not weakness. It is the strongest answer in the room. Do not buy time. If you know, answer. If you do not know, say so, and give me a time.
